name: Amelia Earhart
kicker: Pioneering American aviator · First woman to fly solo across the Atlantic
briefing: Amelia Earhart took her first airplane ride in 1920 and decided right then that she had to fly. In 1932 she became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean, landing in a pasture in Northern Ireland. Five years later, while trying to fly around the world with navigator Fred Noonan, she vanished over the Pacific near tiny Howland Island, and what happened to her has never been proven.

qb.tip: Search QBReader for this answer line (Middle School + Easy High School, power-marked) to see how real tossups clue it.

tossups.p: After crossing the Atlantic as a passenger on the plane _Friendship_ in 1928, this woman said she had been “just baggage, like a sack of potatoes,” because Wilmer Stultz did all the flying. She described that trip in her book _20 Hrs. 40 Min._, named for how long the flight took.
tossups.r: Four years later, she made the crossing alone. For 10 points, name this aviator who later vanished over the Pacific Ocean.

tossups.p: This pilot took off from Harbour Grace, Newfoundland, in a red Lockheed Vega and, after fighting ice and mechanical trouble, landed in a pasture in Northern Ireland. When a farmhand asked if she had flown far, she answered, “From America.”
tossups.r: That 1932 flight came exactly five years after Charles Lindbergh’s. For 10 points, name this first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.

tossups.p: This pilot became the first president of the Ninety-Nines, an organization of women pilots named for its number of charter members. She once took First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt on a night flight from Washington, D.C., to Baltimore while both women wore evening gowns.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aviator who disappeared with navigator Fred Noonan in 1937.

tossups.p: In May 1935, this pilot made the first solo nonstop flight from Mexico City to Newark, New Jersey. Earlier that year, she had become the first person to fly solo from Hawaii to the U.S. mainland, landing in Oakland, California.
tossups.r: In 1932, she had become the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. For 10 points, name this aviator nicknamed “Lady Lindy.”

tossups.p: With about 7,000 miles left in a trip around the world, this pilot took off from Lae, New Guinea, in a twin-engine Lockheed Electra on July 2, 1937. She was headed for Howland Island, a tiny speck in the Pacific where a runway had been built for her.
tossups.r: She and her navigator, Fred Noonan, never arrived. For 10 points, name this aviator whose disappearance is still a mystery.

tossups.p: The Coast Guard cutter _Itasca_ waited at a remote island to guide this pilot by radio, and its crew heard her report, “We must be on you but cannot see you,” and that her fuel was running low. A huge search ordered by President Franklin Roosevelt found no trace of her plane.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aviator who vanished over the Pacific in 1937 with navigator Fred Noonan.

tossups.p: Congress awarded this pilot the Distinguished Flying Cross, making her the first woman to receive it, after a 1932 flight that took about 15 hours. The red Lockheed Vega she flew on that trip is displayed at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aviator, the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic Ocean.

tossups.p: Purdue University hired this pilot to advise women students about careers, and a fund set up through the university helped buy the plane she called her “Flying Laboratory.” Her first try at an around-the-world flight ended in March 1937, when that plane crashed while taking off in Hawaii.
tossups.r: On her second try, she vanished near Howland Island with her navigator, Fred Noonan. For 10 points, name this aviator.

tossups.p: This woman was working as a social worker at Denison House, a settlement house in Boston, when she was invited to join a 1928 flight across the Atlantic. The publisher George Putnam helped choose her for that trip, and the two married in 1931.
tossups.r: In 1932, she made the crossing alone. For 10 points, name this aviator who disappeared over the Pacific in 1937.

tossups.p: As a Red Cross nurse’s aide in Toronto during World War I, this woman watched pilots of the Royal Flying Corps train. In 1920, after a short airplane ride with the pilot Frank Hawks in Long Beach, California, she said she knew she “had to fly.”
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this woman who became the first female pilot to fly solo across the Atlantic.

tossups.p: This pilot took flying lessons from Neta Snook and bought a bright yellow biplane that she nicknamed “The Canary.” In 1922, she flew that plane to 14,000 feet, setting a new altitude record for women.
tossups.r: She later became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. For 10 points, name this pilot who disappeared in 1937.

tossups.p: Some researchers believe that this pilot landed on Nikumaroro [“nee-koo-mah-ROH-roh”], then called Gardner Island, and lived there for a time as a castaway, but no one has proven it. Others think her plane ran out of fuel and sank into the ocean.
tossups.r: She vanished in 1937 while flying with navigator Fred Noonan. For 10 points, name this aviator who tried to fly around the world.

tossups.p: This author wrote the memoir _The Fun of It_, and her husband later gathered her notes from a final trip into the book _Last Flight_. Born in Atchison, Kansas, she was nicknamed “Lady Lindy” because reporters thought she looked like a famous male pilot.
tossups.r: For 10 points, name this aviator who was the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic.

tossups.p: This pilot launched her own line of clothing and a brand of lightweight luggage that carried her name. In August 1932, she became the first woman to fly solo nonstop across the United States, from Los Angeles to Newark, New Jersey.
tossups.r: Months earlier, she had flown solo across the Atlantic. For 10 points, name this aviator who disappeared in 1937.

tossups.p: This pilot finished third in the 1929 Women’s Air Derby, a race from Santa Monica, California, to Cleveland that the humorist Will Rogers nicknamed the “Powder Puff Derby.” Later that year, she helped found an organization of women pilots.
tossups.r: In 1937, she disappeared over the Pacific while trying to fly around the world. For 10 points, name this aviator.

Disappeared over the Pacific Ocean in 1937 while trying to fly around the world
Her navigator on that last flight was Fred Noonan
Nicknamed “Lady Lindy” because reporters thought she looked like Charles Lindbergh

Took off from Lae, New Guinea, on July 2, 1937, with about 7,000 miles to go

The Coast Guard cutter _Itasca_ heard her last messages: “We must be on you but cannot see you”
Unproven theories: her plane ran out of fuel and sank, or she was a castaway on Nikumaroro (Gardner Island)
First president of the Ninety-Nines, an organization of women pilots (founded 1929)
First woman to receive the Distinguished Flying Cross (1932); her red Vega is at the Smithsonian
Was a social worker at Denison House, a Boston settlement house, when she was picked for the 1928 flight
Red Cross nurse’s aide in Toronto during World War I, where she watched Royal Flying Corps pilots

Learned from Neta Snook; her yellow plane “The Canary” set a women’s altitude record of 14,000 feet (1922)
Books: _20 Hrs. 40 Min._ and _The Fun of It_; _Last Flight_ came out after she vanished

First woman to fly solo nonstop across the U.S. (1932); first solo nonstop flight from Mexico City to Newark (1935)
Born in Atchison, Kansas (1897)

trap.title: Lady Lindy, not Lindy
trap.body: Her nickname “Lady Lindy” and a 1932 Atlantic flight that came exactly five years after Charles Lindbergh’s make the two pilots easy to mix up. Lindbergh made the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic in 1927, in the _Spirit of St. Louis_; she was the first woman to fly it solo. Other pioneer women pilots appear too: Harriet Quimby was the first woman to fly across the English Channel (1912), and Bessie Coleman was the first African American woman to earn a pilot’s license.
trap.fix: Listen for “she” and for her last flight: Howland Island, Fred Noonan, the Lockheed Electra, and 1937 all mean her. The _Spirit of St. Louis_ and landing in Paris mean Lindbergh. Say her last name, since “Amelia” alone only earns a prompt.
